Ahead of Thanksgiving, more Americans struggle to put food on the table
Andreas Leal and his wife peruse the shelves at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas. Food banks and pantries across the country are experiencing surging demand amid declining federal food assistance and higher grocery prices. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards.
As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and the hodgepodge of donated items on the toiletry shelves. A 75-year-old retiree, Leal said every bit helps when trying to keep up with rising prices.
“It’s very expensive,” he said. “Everything is expensive right now.”
Leal said his monthly Social Security benefit can’t keep up with rising costs. While the federal program boosted benefits by 2.8% this year, he said he just received notice that his residential property tax bill will jump 30%, costing him some $600. The increases require constant trade-offs. For example, to save on gas, the couple forgoes trips to visit their son who lives about 45 minutes away.
Leaders of Cross-Lines Community Outreach say such stories are more and more common. Its Community Market, a food pantry resembling a grocery store, serves about 1,900 families per month — a 35% increase over last year.
“Daily, we have to turn people away,” said Executive Director Susila Jones.
The market previously aimed to provide a couple pounds of frozen ground beef each month to every family. But those costs are now too high, pushing Cross-Lines to buy ground turkey or chicken — if prices are low enough.
Cross-Lines serves people across Wyandotte County, one of the most populous counties in Kansas with a poverty rate that exceeds state and national averages. In recent years, the food pantry has become more lenient about its income requirements and welcomed people who seek aid from multiple organizations.
“This is not what people want to do and so we really just let people come to us when they need to come to us,” she said. “Because we know even if you are working, if you’ve had steady income, just one paycheck can put you over the edge.”
Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance. At the same time, those charitable organizations are seeing a wave of Americans who have lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the nation’s largest food assistance program.
About 5.5 million Americans have lost SNAP benefits since last July’s passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut taxes and federal safety net programs. The law changed SNAP eligibility rules, ended certain work requirement exemptions and shifted new costs to states that administer the federal program.
More people are expected to lose SNAP aid as the legislation is fully implemented in the coming years. And earlier this month, the Trump administration proposed enrollment rule changes that would cut eligibility for another 6.3 million people.
Without congressional action, few experts see much relief ahead, further stressing the nation’s patchwork of churches, food banks and nonprofits laboring to keep people fed.

Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year.
He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit, multiple media reported on Thursday.
The role still requires formal appointment after consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, but neither has veto power and the decision follows intense political wrangling to reach a consensus on who should serve the eight-year term.
Reuters reported that de Cos was set for the nomination after the Netherlands agreed to back Klaas Knot, the only other candidate, citing European diplomatic sources.
De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024.
He chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024, and has been General Manager of the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements since July 2025.
Both de Cos and his main rival for the ECB top job, Knot, were widely seen as candidates with deep knowledge and experience in monetary policy and financial stability — attributes that took on particular importance at a time of resurgent inflation, fragmentation and political uncertainty.
Lagarde had extensive experience in financial institutions but was criticized by some early in her tenure for a lack of central banking experience.
De Cos gained sufficient political backing in closed-door discussions and negotiations since Lagarde said she would step down on Feb. 7, 2027, over seven years after she became the first woman to helm the ECB. That was despite a final push by the Netherlands at the European Council meeting this week backing Knot.
Representatives from the euro area's biggest economies — Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands — have been horse-trading as they look to secure representation on the central bank's six-member Executive Board.
Influential roles as chief economist, expected to go to Germany's Markus Brunnermeier, and head of the Markets Portfolio, for which France's Laurence Boone has reportedly been tapped, also change hands in 2027.
Not a dove, not a hawk, but an 'owl'
Analysts say de Cos's commentary and actions over more than two decades at Spain's central bank paint him as moderately dovish — inclined to favor lower interest rates to support economic growth — but also as a pragmatist who has been willing to adapt.
That has included support for strong rate hikes during the energy price shock that followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but also giving staunch backing for rates below zero and the huge stimulus package launched by then-ECB President Mario Draghi to reboot the euro zone economy in 2019.
De Cos quipped in 2024 that he was an "owl" after being asked if he was a hawk or a dove, emphasizing his focus on data and the situation at hand.

While that not only leads to suboptimal performance, it can also increase your risk of injury, he explains.

If you swapped part of your savings for a fixed monthly cheque, you bought certainty about one thing: the dollar amount. Nothing in that deal protects what those dollars buy. The cost is easy to miss, because the cheque itself never changes. Over 20 years a flat cheque lost 40.2% of its buying power. Over the same years, the dividend on $1 million of Procter & Gamble shares bought in 2006 rose every year, from $21,407 to $68,036.
Take a flat cheque of $21,407 a year. US consumer prices rose 67.2% from October 2006 to October 2026. By the end, that same cheque bought only what $12,807 bought at the start. It had lost 40.2% of its buying power. Even the last 10 years alone saw prices rise 39.6%.
The fixed cheque still does its main job well. It arrives on schedule, it does not depend on a stock price, and you never have to decide what to sell to pay a bill. For a retiree, that calm is worth something. The catch: a cheque that felt generous in year one of retirement covers less of the bills each year after.

In their first year those shares paid $21,407 in dividends. That is why the flat cheque above has exactly that size. That is 217.8% more than in the first year, while consumer prices rose 67.2%. Over the 20 years the dividends added up to $878,997, against $428,144 from the flat cheque. The holder also still owns the shares, worth $2,726,743 at the November 25 close.
Does the gap show up over a shorter stretch?
A retiree who started a decade ago saw the same pattern on a smaller scale. Shares bought with $1 million at the close of $83.46 on November 25, 2016 paid $32,810 in their first year of dividends. A flat cheque of that size has since lost 28.4% of its buying power. The dividend on those shares rose to $51,789, a gain of 57.8% against a 39.6% rise in prices.
What did the rising cheque cost?
The price of a rising cheque is the ride. Procter & Gamble’s worst fall in the 20 years was 40.8%, from its close on Wednesday, December 12, 2007 to Monday, March 9, 2009. On paper, the holding shrank from $1,175,350 to $695,419. The dividends kept coming through it, $30,694 over that stretch, and the quarterly rate rose from $0.35 to $0.40 a share.

China's industrial profits in October grew at their fastest pace since May, supported by an AI-driven electronics boom and higher energy prices, while consumer-facing industries squeezed by weak demand continued to be a drag.
Profits at sizeable industrial firms surged 20.1% in October from a year earlier, according to data released Friday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first 10 months this year, the earnings grew 16% year on year, having risen 15.5% through September.
That extends a notable rebound in 2026 after three years of declines followed by a tepid 0.6% growth last year, with profits on track to log their strongest annual expansion since 2021.
Despite the sharp headline figure, "the recovery has yet to broaden into a more durable improvement in corporate profitability," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, as the rebound was largely led by upstream sectors amid higher energy prices.
China's economy has been running at two speeds, with AI-related manufacturing and exports powering growth while household consumption has been lagging. Retail sales grew a smaller-than-expected 0.4% in October, and fixed-asset investment steepened declines to 8.1% in the first 10 months.
Profit gains were concentrated in a set of sectors tied to the global AI buildout and higher commodity prices, while consumer-facing manufacturers struggled to pass on higher input costs, squeezing margins.
Earnings in the electronics sector doubled in the first 10 months from the same period last year, as demand for AI computing power lifted memory chips and related manufacturing, said Yu Weining, chief statistician of the NBS.
Profits in high-tech manufacturing jumped 50.9%, outpacing the industry as a whole, Yu added. Makers of spacecraft and launch vehicles reported a 63.2% rise.
Commodity producers also saw sharp growth in profits as demand tied to renewable energy and AI pushed up copper and aluminum prices, Yu said. Petroleum processors swung to a combined profit from a loss a year earlier.

Two things are happening in trail running and ultrarunning at the same time: More athletes are talking openly about anxiety, depression, burnout, and eating disorders. And more are hiring someone to help them race with better focus, confidence, and composure.
Both are great. The trouble is that we’ve started treating them as the same thing, and they aren’t.
Mental health and mental performance overlap, but they call for different kinds of help. When runners can’t tell them apart, they end up in the wrong office. The athlete who needs help with performance skills spends months in talk therapy, or the athlete with depression gets handed a visualization script.
Confusing mental health with mental performance, and vice versa, costs people time, money, and sometimes their well-being. Ultrarunning already has plenty of ways to burn all three without adding this to the pile.
Mental Health Versus Mental Performance
Mental health is about how you function as a person: your mood, anxiety, sleep, relationships, relationship with food and your body, and capacity to get through an ordinary Tuesday. Clinical work here — diagnosing and treating depression, anxiety disorders, eating disorders, trauma, and substance use — belongs to licensed professionals: psychologists, psychiatrists, counselors, and clinical social workers. This is not the realm of your coach, a podcast host, or the person at the aid station with strong opinions about mantras.
Mental performance focuses on how you execute a specific task under specific demands: pacing a 50 miler, staying composed when the weather turns on you, managing your attention at hour nine of an ultra, or bouncing back from a DNF. The work is skills-based and educational. Think of it as strength training for your attention and self-talk, not clinical treatment.
However, the two do share a border. Anxiety management shows up in both, and someone who’s in a good place psychologically may be better positioned to train and race well. But maybe not.
Mental health and performance answer different questions. Mental health asks, “Are you ok?” Mental performance asks, “What do you need to be able to do, and how do we build that skill?”
The sport psychology field has wrestled with this differentiation for years, and the answer keeps coming back the same. The European Federation of Sports Psychology (FEPSAC) position statement on athlete mental health calls for clear models of service provision because the roles between mental health support and mental performance consulting are distinct and the risks of blurring them are real (1). A later international consensus statement made a similar case: Improving athlete mental health takes qualified, coordinated care, not a general-purpose “mindset” approach (2).
Dr. Lara Pence, a licensed clinical psychologist who works with professional and elite athletes, frames the difference as functioning versus performance. Mental health asks, “Am I functioning at a certain level that allows me to show up for myself, in relationships, and in the world?” Performance, she says, “is much more about dialing into a specific aspect, with one’s mind as the priority.”

Investing.com -- Bank of America kept its forecast for Brent crude at an average of $80 a barrel in 2027, telling investors in a note that geopolitics will remain the main driver of oil prices.
The bank sees West Texas Intermediate averaging $74.
"Looking into 2027, geopolitics will remain at the center of oil price formation," commodity strategist Francisco Blanch wrote in the bank's 2027 energy outlook.
Brent front-month futures have averaged about $91 a barrel so far in 2026 because of record supply disruptions. The low point was $60 at the start of the year and the high was $118 in March, when the U.S. and Israel struck Iran.
BofA sees three possible paths for oil next year: a peace deal, a continuation of the fragile status quo, or renewed kinetic war.
"Given the U.S. midterm election results, we maintain our $80/bbl Brent crude oil forecast as a baseline, which is a combination of the status quo and an increasingly touted peace deal," Blanch said.
Oil demand could rebound by 3 million barrels a day in 2027 as world growth expands, assuming supply is restored, according to the bank.
BofA named a solid peace deal, weaker economic growth and an OPEC+ price war as the main downside risks. It said three factors could hold Brent at a floor of around $70 if those risks play out: limited growth in U.S. shale output, the need to rebuild strategic stocks and stronger buying from consumers at lower prices.
"To the upside, Brent prices are unlikely to average more than $130/bbl due to demand destruction, but spikes above $150 can't be ruled out if war in the Middle East broadens," Blanch added.
BofA also kept its 2027 Henry Hub natural gas forecast at $3.35 per million British thermal units. It expects Europe's TTF gas benchmark to average €55 per megawatt hour.

Jensen Huang is back at the helm, and Nvidia's (NVDA) bull case remains in play. Nvidia shares surged 31.5% on November 23 after news of Jensen Huang's reinstatement, underscoring how closely investor confidence in the company is tied to its co-founder.
While near-term volatility is likely to persist, I remain decisively Bullish over the long term. Nvidia makes the chips, networking gear, and software powering the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, and its earnings story is strong enough to ride out the ups and downs.
Huang's Return Restores Continuity, but Not Trust
Huang's return restores strategic continuity, but it does not restore trust overnight. Nvidia disclosed on November 12 that its co-founder and chief executive officer (CEO) had resigned after the board accepted his resignation on November 11. The stock finished that session 4.3% lower. On November 23, Nvidia announced that Huang had been reinstated, and the shares rose 31.5%.
The episode highlighted a degree of key-person risk that I had underestimated. Nvidia's product cadence and customer confidence have always been closely tied to Huang. His return obviously removes the immediate succession problem. However, it leaves investors with a governance question.
The board reinstated him before completing its independent investigation, shortly after creating a National Security and Export Control Committee on November 17 and alongside launching a search for a Chief Compliance Officer. Those oversight steps are the right moves, but they do not excuse reversing a major leadership decision before the facts are settled.
For my Bullish thesis, Huang's return is a stabilizer, though stronger governance is still required.
Nvidia's Earnings Still Point to Powerful AI Demand
Nvidia's results still point to very strong AI demand, and that's the part of the argument I find most compelling. Q3 FY2027 revenue was up 103% year-over-year to $115.8 billion, and Data Center revenue was up 110% to $107.6 billion. GAAP diluted earnings per share (EPS) came in at $2.70. Management has guided to around $130 billion in Q4 FY2027 revenue, plus or minus 3%, all the way through the end of the year, despite assuming zero Data Center compute revenue from China.
